summary: For ages 13–14, this guidance teaches bivariate data on scatter graphs: describing the trend between two variables as positive, negative, or no correlation; drawing a line of best fit and using it to predict within the data range; and, most importantly, separating correlation from causation. Three load-bearing ideas: (1) correlation is a trend across a cloud of points, and strength means how tightly points cluster around a line, NOT how steep the line is; (2) correlation is not causation — co-variation can arise from direct cause, a common cause (confounder), reverse cause, or coincidence; (3) people tend to see the correlation they expect ('illusory correlation'), over-reading expected links and under-reading surprising ones. Activities ground every example in real, meaningful pairs and repeatedly ask 'what else could explain this link?' A live scatter sandbox with a confounder slider is the primary proposed mechanism; a Socratic sceptic, a scorable check, a static annotated gallery, and a predict-observe-explain task are preserved as distinct complementary approaches.
misconceptions: Treating correlation as proof of causation — assuming that because two variables move together, one must cause the other
'Illusory correlation' — seeing or overstating a relationship because a causal link is expected, and dismissing one that isn't
Confusing the strength of correlation with the steepness of the line (thinking a steeper line means stronger correlation)
Treating negative correlation as 'no correlation' (or as 'bad'), rather than as a genuine downward relationship

activities.title: Scatter sandbox: tighten the cloud, then toggle a confounder
steps: Drag points on a scatter graph and watch a live 'strength' read-out and a best-fit line update as you move them.

Stretch the whole cloud vertically (scale every y-value by the same factor) so the trend line gets steeper and the spread around it grows in proportion, and notice that the strength read-out stays the same; then pull the points closer to the line without changing its steepness and watch the strength increase.

Move a single 'temperature' slider and watch it simultaneously push ice-cream sales UP and beach-swimming/drownings UP, so a strong positive correlation appears between ice cream and drownings even though neither causes the other.
Turn the temperature slider back down and watch both variables fall together, showing that in this model, where temperature is built in as the common cause, the hidden variable drives both.

For fresh correlated pairs, use a 'what else could explain this?' prompt to name any plausible confounder, and decide which of four explanations seems most plausible for each pair, giving a reason: direct cause, common cause, reverse cause, coincidence.
activities.insight: Strength of correlation is how closely points hug the line, not how steep the line is; and a real, strong correlation can exist between two variables when a hidden third variable drives both — so correlation alone never proves causation.

activities.title: Argue it out with a sceptical scientist
steps: Respond to a character who presents tempting causal claims drawn from correlations, e.g. 'Towns with more churches have more crime — so do churches cause crime?' or 'More firefighters are sent to bigger fires and there is more damage — so should we send fewer firefighters?'
For each claim, explain in your own words what ELSE could account for the link besides one variable causing the other, and try to name the confounding common cause (e.g. town population; fire size).
When pressed, state whether the correlation is real, and separately whether the causal claim follows from it.
activities.insight: Correlation-vs-causation is an argument you can make: a real link can be explained by a confounder, reverse cause, or coincidence, so you must give a reason rather than accept the causal story.

activities.title: Predict-observe-explain: the firefighters data
steps: Study data in which the number of firefighters sent to a fire is strongly positively correlated with the amount of damage caused.

Before any discussion, WRITE your prediction and your REASON for this question: 'If the fire service sent FEWER firefighters to each fire, would there be less damage?' Commit to both prediction and reason first.
Then observe the lurking variable — the SIZE of the fire — which drives both the firefighters sent and the damage, and compare it against your written reason.
Finally, transfer the reasoning to a fresh pair: explain what could cause BOTH ice-cream sales and drownings to rise and fall together.
activities.insight: A correlation can be fully real yet not show the effect of one variable on the other, because a confounding variable (fire size; hot weather) drives both measured quantities — so changing one variable need not change the other in the way the correlation suggests (sending fewer firefighters would likely mean more damage, not less).

activities.title: Scorable check: type, strength, and causal claims
steps: Sort scatter graphs into positive, negative, or no correlation, each anchored in a real context.

Compare two scatters for strength, drawn on the same axes, including a pair where one has a steeper line but points widely scattered around it and the other a gentler line with points hugging it closely (so the gentler one clearly has the stronger correlation) — choose which shows the STRONGER correlation.
Answer a two-tier causal item: first 'Does this correlation prove X causes Y?' and then 'Why / why not?', explaining your reasoning.
activities.insight: You can reliably identify correlation type, judge strength by clustering rather than gradient, and reject an unwarranted causal claim with a stated reason.

activities.title: Annotated scatter gallery (reference)
steps: View three canonical scatter clouds side by side — positive, negative, and no correlation — and reveal each one's correlation type.
Examine a confounded pair (ice-cream sales vs drownings) and reveal the hidden common cause (hot weather).
Compare two scatters that share the same gradient line but have very different amounts of scatter, and view a line of best fit used to read a predicted value within the data range.
activities.insight: The three correlation types, the strength-vs-steepness distinction, and a worked confounded example can be recognised and named as reference points.

checkQuestion: Pose the claim, then ask for the reason. Tier 1: 'Across the year, ice-cream sales and the number of people who drown at the beach rise and fall together — they are strongly positively correlated. Does buying more ice cream CAUSE more drownings?' Tier 2: 'Explain your reasoning — how do you account for the fact that they go up and down together?' Read it aloud and listen; do not offer options.
checkAnswer: Tier 1: No. Tier 2: because correlation is not causation — a third, confounding variable (hot/summer weather) drives BOTH ice-cream sales and how many people swim (and so drown); the two are linked through a common cause, not because one causes the other. A full answer names the confounder and states that variables moving together does not by itself establish that one causes the other.
